title: Meeting new friends at an asado in Buenos Aires
setting: It's Sunday afternoon on a rooftop terrace in Palermo, Buenos Aires. Your friend Martina has invited you to an asado (barbecue) with her friends. The grill is smoking, music is playing, and a mate gourd is going around the group.
objectives: Use "vos" the way people do in Argentina
Introduce yourself and ask where someone is from
Follow the basic etiquette of sharing mate
varietyNote: This is Rioplatense Spanish, spoken in and around Buenos Aires (and in Uruguay). It uses "vos" instead of "tú", and many people pronounce "ll" and "y" with a "sh" sound ("calle" sounds like "cashe"). Other regions of Argentina have their own accents and expressions — Córdoba, for example, has a very distinctive one.

phrases.translation: How's it going? (literally "What are you doing?")
phrases.exampleTranslation: Hi! How's it going? All good?
phrases.note: A very common casual greeting in Argentina — it isn't really asking what you're doing.

phrases.exampleTranslation: And you, where are you from?
phrases.note: "Sos" is the "vos" form of "ser" (to be): vos sos = tú eres.

alsoHeard.where: With "tú" — used in Spain, Mexico and many other countries

phrases.note: The all-purpose Argentine "OK". In Spain you'd more often hear "vale".
"Querés" is the "vos" form of "querer" (tú quieres). Vos forms are usually stressed on the last syllable: tenés, sabés, podés.

phrases.exampleTranslation: Hey, can you pass me the salad?
phrases.note: So typical of Argentina and Uruguay that "che" became a nickname for Argentines abroad.
"Re" is a very common informal intensifier in Argentina, like "really" or "super".

cultureNotes: In Argentina, "vos" replaces "tú" in everyday speech, with its own verb forms (vos sos, vos tenés, vos querés). Using "tú" is perfectly understood — it just sounds like you're from somewhere else.
Mate is shared from one gourd. One person (the "cebador") prepares it and hands it to each person in turn. Drink it all, then hand it back to the cebador.
Saying "gracias" when you hand back the mate means "no more for me, thanks". Don't say it until you've had enough!
A single kiss on the cheek is a common greeting among friends — including, often, between men.
At an asado, it's a tradition to applaud the person who cooked the meat: "¡Un aplauso para el asador!"

steps.text: Martina brings you over to a group chatting near the grill.

steps.speaker: Martina
steps.text: ¡Che, chicos! Les presento a alguien que conocí en Lingua Bud.
steps.translation: Hey, everyone! Let me introduce someone I met on Lingua Bud.

steps.speaker: Facu
steps.translation: Hi! How's it going? Where are you from?

options.text: How it's going, and where you're from
options.why: "¿Qué hacés?" is a casual "How's it going?", and "¿De dónde sos?" means "Where are you from?" (vos sos = tú eres).

options.text: What you're doing, and who you are
options.why: "¿Qué hacés?" is just a greeting here, not a real question about what you're doing. And "Who are you?" would be "¿Quién sos?".

options.text: What you do for work, and where you're going
options.why: Work would be "¿A qué te dedicás?", and "Where are you going?" would be "¿Adónde vas?".

steps.text: You tell him where you're from. Now you want to ask him the same question — like a local.

steps.prompt: How do you ask Facu where he's from, Buenos Aires–style?

options.why: Perfect — "vos" with "sos" is exactly how people say it here.
Completely correct Spanish and everyone will understand you. It just sounds like you learned Spanish from Spain or Mexico — here people use "vos".
"Usted" is too formal for a friend's barbecue. Save it for older people or formal situations.

steps.speaker: Facu
steps.text: Soy de Córdoba, pero vivo acá hace años. ¿Querés un mate?
steps.translation: I'm from Córdoba, but I've lived here for years. Do you want some mate?

steps.prompt: You'd love to try it. How do you say yes, the Argentine way?

options.why: "Dale" is the go-to Argentine "sure!".
That's how you'd say it in Spain. People will understand, but it marks you as having learned Spanish from Spain.
Correct, but it sounds stiff and formal — like agreeing to a business proposal, not a drink with friends.

steps.text: Facu hands you the gourd. You drink the warm, slightly bitter mate through the metal straw. It's good — you'd happily have another round later.

steps.prompt: You've finished the mate and want to stay in the round. What do you do?

options.text: Hand it back to Facu without saying "gracias" yet.
options.why: Right. In a mate round, "gracias" means "no more for me". Save it for when you've had enough.

options.text: Say "¡Gracias!" warmly as you hand it back.
options.why: Polite everywhere else, but here "gracias" tells the cebador you're done — you might get skipped next round!

options.text: Stir it with the straw and pass it to the person next to you.
options.why: Two classic mistakes: don't move the straw (it can block it), and hand the mate back to the cebador, who passes it on.

steps.speaker: Martina
steps.text: ¡Chicos, la carne está lista! ¡Un aplauso para el asador!
steps.translation: Everyone, the meat is ready! A round of applause for the grill master!

steps.prompt: Everyone starts clapping toward the person at the grill. What's going on?

options.text: It's a tradition to applaud the "asador" who cooked the meat — join in!
options.why: Exactly. Applauding the asador is a much-loved part of any Argentine barbecue.

options.text: Someone has a birthday — you should start singing.
options.why: It's not a birthday — the applause is for whoever spent hours at the grill.

options.text: They're being sarcastic because the meat took so long.
options.why: It's genuine! The asador is the star of the afternoon.

steps.speaker: Facu
steps.text: ¿Y? ¿Qué te parece? La carne está re buena, ¿no?
steps.translation: So? What do you think? The meat is really good, isn't it?

options.why: "Re" is a common informal intensifier in Argentina — like "really" or "super".
In words like "rehacer" (to redo), "re-" means "again" — but on its own before an adjective, Argentines use it to mean "really".
It's the opposite — "re" makes it stronger, not weaker.

steps.prompt: You want to agree enthusiastically, like Facu would. What do you say?

options.text: ¡Sí, está re buena! ¡Un aplauso para el asador!
options.why: Perfect — you're using "re" like a local and joining in the tradition.
"Otra vez" means "again", so this sounds like the meat is good *again* — a confusing compliment.
Close! But "la carne" is feminine, so it's "buena". And for how food tastes right now, "está" is more natural than "es".
